name: Sedating and non-sedating antihistamines
summary: The NHS describes non-sedating antihistamines such as cetirizine as less likely to cause drowsiness than sedating ones such as chlorphenamine.
keyPoints: Antihistamines block histamine, the chemical that triggers itching, sneezing and watery eyes during an allergic reaction.
Cetirizine, loratadine and fexofenadine are called non-sedating, while chlorphenamine (Piriton) is a sedating antihistamine.
Non-sedating does not mean never drowsy: the NHS says some people still find cetirizine sedating, and it advises care with driving and alcohol.
The NHS says chlorphenamine can be taken in pregnancy and a non-drowsy antihistamine such as loratadine may be suggested instead.
A pharmacist or GP can advise on choosing an antihistamine; NHS 111 is for urgent advice, and 999 is for signs of a serious allergic reaction.

body.heading: What do antihistamines do?
body.body:
Antihistamines are medicines that block the effects of histamine. Histamine is a chemical that the body makes when it meets something it is allergic to, such as pollen or animal fur. It is what sets off allergy symptoms such as itching, sneezing and watery eyes.

People mostly use them for allergy problems such as hay fever.

body.heading: Which antihistamines are sedating and which are not?
body.body:
Antihistamines are often sorted into two groups, called sedating and non-sedating. Sedating means more likely to cause sleepiness, and non-sedating means less likely.

A hospital leaflet from Cambridge University Hospitals names cetirizine, loratadine and fexofenadine as non-sedating tablets that usually do not cause drowsiness, so they can be used in the daytime. Chlorphenamine, which is sold as Piriton, is a sedating antihistamine. The NHS groups it with other sedating antihistamines such as cinnarizine and promethazine.

The Cambridge leaflet says every antihistamine can cause some drowsiness, though it is much more likely with a sedating one. The NHS says cetirizine is less likely to cause sleepiness than sedating antihistamines such as chlorphenamine, but more likely to do so than loratadine, desloratadine or fexofenadine.

body.heading: What side effects can they cause?
body.body:
For cetirizine, the NHS lists feeling sleepy and tired as the most common side effect. Headaches, dry mouth, feeling sick, dizziness and diarrhoea are also listed. The NHS adds that some people find cetirizine sedating even though it is classed as non-drowsy.

For chlorphenamine, the NHS lists drowsiness during the day, feeling sick, dizziness or trouble concentrating, dry mouth, headaches and blurred vision. It says children and people over 65 are more likely to have some side effects, such as feeling restless or excited.

The NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 about yellowing of the skin or eyes, unusual bruising or bleeding, or difficulty passing urine while using chlorphenamine. A pharmacist or GP can answer non-urgent questions about side effects.

body.heading: What do the NHS and hospital leaflets say about driving and alcohol?
body.body:
For cetirizine, the NHS says not to drive or ride a bike if it makes a person sleepy. If someone is unsure, the NHS says to ask a doctor or pharmacist. The NHS also says it is best not to drink alcohol while taking cetirizine, because it can add to sleepiness. The Cambridge leaflet makes the same point, saying that tablets such as cetirizine can enhance the effects of alcohol.

For chlorphenamine, the NHS advises not to drive or use machinery after taking it. The NHS also notes that some liquid products contain a small amount of alcohol, so the packaging is worth checking.

body.heading: What about pregnancy, breastfeeding and children?
body.body:
The NHS says chlorphenamine can be taken in pregnancy and that there is no good evidence it harms the baby. It can cause drowsiness, so a doctor or pharmacist may suggest a non-drowsy antihistamine such as loratadine. A summary of NHS antihistamine guidance also says loratadine is usually recommended when an antihistamine is needed in pregnancy.

For breastfeeding, NHS guidance says loratadine or cetirizine are usually fine. The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service prefers non-sedating antihistamines and suggests watching the baby for drowsiness, irritability, dry mouth, poor feeding and poor weight gain. It says younger babies who are fed only breast milk are at greater risk of side effects. For chlorphenamine, the NHS says to contact NHS 111 or a healthcare professional if a breastfed baby feeds poorly or seems unusually sleepy or irritable.

For children, the NHS says most adults and children aged 1 year or over can take chlorphenamine, but it is not suitable for everyone. It lists extra care for people with conditions such as glaucoma, epilepsy, asthma, heart disease, an enlarged prostate, or liver or kidney problems. One NHS formulary summary notes that age limits differ between products, so a pharmacist can help with what suits a child.

body.heading: When should someone get advice, and when is it an emergency?
body.body:
For everyday questions, such as which antihistamine suits a person or how a side effect is behaving, a pharmacist or GP is the usual route. NHS 111 can give urgent advice, for example about the symptoms listed above or a breastfed baby who is unusually sleepy.

The NHS says to call 999 for signs of a serious allergic reaction. These include swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, a tight throat or trouble swallowing, and blue, grey or pale lips or skin. They also include sudden confusion or extreme drowsiness, and fainting without recovery. In children, a limp or unresponsive state is another warning sign. The NHS also says to call 999 or go to A&E for signs of taking too much, such as a racing or irregular heartbeat, seizures or hallucinations.
